newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai baht stands ground after float, bourse soars.
newsitem.headline: Thai baht stands ground after float, bourse soars.

text.p: The Thai baht stood its ground on Thursday, a day after its effective devaluation, while share prices spurted further ahead as foreign investors decided Thailand's financial woes may be ending.
At 0930 GMT, the baht was quoted offshore at 29.00/29.500 to the dollar -- just above the first reference rate set for it by the Bank of Thailand under its new managed float regime.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh welcomed the baht's relative stability and a rise of nearly 17 percent in Thai share prices since the float was announced on Wednesday.

"We have seen a substantial capital inflow into the (stock) market. Despite earlier expectation of a (wide) baht swing, it holds out well in its quick adjustment. Today's rate is in line with what we have expected," he said.
Analysts said that although the new reference rate for the baht was a bit firm, the currency should manage to hover near those levels for the rest of 1997 as Thai business weathers the shock.
"A lot would depend on post-float economic indicators for July, which should come out in September," said Charl Kengchon of the Thai Farmers Research Institute.
"Only then can the market see its impact on foreign capital flow and gauge business adjustment to the initial pains," he said.

The baht initially dived by around 20 percent in offshore markets on news of the float. Its new daily reference, based on the previous day's trading levels, is only six percent weaker than pre-float levels onshore.
Elsewhere in Southeast Asia, shock waves from the float dissipated, but both the Singapore dollar and Philippine peso came under fresh speculative attack.
The head of research at SocGen-Crosby Securites in Singapore told reporters the peso was overvalued and likely to slip another five to six percent this year.
In Bangkok, foreign exchange analysts said the Thai authorities were clearly not ready to let the baht fall too far, too fast.
With capital controls still in place, the offshore market will remain illiquid and a dangerous place to speculate against the baht, but over time offshore and onshore rates will converge, they said.
Thailand's central bank raised interest rates by two percentage points to 12.50 percent to prevent a baht meltdown and has pledged to defend the currency at its new levels.
The Thai stock market, which closed nearly eight percent up on Wednesday, climbed another 8.65 percent to close at 617.98 on Thursday as foreign investors led the rush to buy stocks.
"This is amazing," said a foreign analyst. "When people pile in they really want in and don't care. There are still a lot of orders coming in from overseas."
The Thai market, which was mired in eight-year lows for most of the past two months, has gained nearly 90 points in the past two days and moved to levels not seen since early May.
But economists warned that it would probably be months before Thailand's economy, mired in its worst slump for more than a decade, could be given a clean bill of health.
Interest rates had to fall to spur growth and the finance sector, burdened with non-performing property loans, faced further pain as mergers ordered by the government took place, they said.
In addition, the country's swollen trade deficit was likely to widen as the fall in the baht's value raises import bills and fans domestic inflation.

Growth in gross domestic product is expected to fall well below five percent, down from 6.4 percent in 1996. At the same time, many Thai corporates, unprotected from exchange fluctuations, face mounting costs in servicing their foreign debt.
The Thai Rating and Information Services agency said on Thursday it had placed all Thai firms and debt instruments rated by it on CreditAlert with "negative" implications.

"Unless more significant changes are made in the next two to three months, this tank of oxygen could be used up and Thailand could be in a worse position," said Kenneth Courtis, chief economist at Deutsche Bank Group Asia Pacific.
Most analysts -- and even government officials -- acknowledge that it will be early 1998 before the Thai economy is out of the woods.

"There should not be much more of the very bitter medicines left but there will of course be more strong measures that the government will take in coming months," said former finance minister Surakiart Sathirathai.
"I see light at the end of the tunnel within one year," said Surakiart, who is adviser to the prime minister.
The International Monetary Fund has welcomed the Thai baht float and rate rise, saying it would respond rapidly to a Thai request for technical support.
